analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for bank regulators to block consumer protection rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Financial Services Committee and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it much easier for the Financial Stability Oversight Council — a panel of federal bank regulators — to strike down rules issued by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. It would have lowered the vote needed to block a rule from two-thirds to a simple majority (excluding the CFPB Director), made blocking mandatory once a member agency objected, and loosened the standard from rules that risk the whole banking system to any rule "inconsistent with the safe and sound operations" of U.S. financial institutions. It also would have required the CFPB to weigh the impact of its rules on banks' financial soundness when writing them. The bill was referred to committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, large banks and other financial institutions would have gained a powerful lever: any member agency could petition to kill a CFPB rule, and the Council would have been required to set it aside on a simple majority vote using a much easier test. Rules on mortgages, credit cards, debt collection, and payday lending could have been overridden by regulators whose mandate is bank health, not consumer protection. The CFPB's own Director would have been excluded from the vote on its rules.

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the vote needed for the Financial Stability Oversight Council to stay or set aside a CFPB regulation from two-thirds of the Council to a simple majority, with the CFPB Director excluded from voting.

Turns the Council's set-aside power from optional into mandatory: upon any member agency's petition, the Council 'shall' set aside a final CFPB rule it finds inconsistent with the safe and sound operations of U.S. financial institutions — a far easier test than the current standard that the rule must put the safety and soundness of the U.S. banking system or the stability of the financial system at risk.

Repeals the deadlines that currently force dismissal of a set-aside petition if the Council does not act in time, and removes the bar on setting aside a rule after the statutory window closes, so challenges to CFPB rules could persist or arrive at any time.

Requires the CFPB Director to consider the impact of any proposed rule on the financial safety or soundness of insured depository institutions — effectively adding a bank-profitability checkpoint to consumer rulewriting.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who rely on CFPB rules — mortgage borrowers, credit card holders, people facing debt collectors or payday lenders — would bear the risk of having those protections struck down by bank regulators. The CFPB itself would lose much of its independent rulemaking authority, since its rules could be overridden by a panel dominated by banking regulators.

drawbacks.text: The real cost of the bill would have fallen on consumer protections: under the new 'safe and sound operations' standard, a rule that protects consumers but trims profits at individual banks could be voided, even if it posed no risk to the banking system as a whole — the opposite of the current system-wide risk test.

Supporters' best-faith argument was accountability: the CFPB is led by a single director, funded outside the appropriations process, and its rules cover nearly all consumer finance, so giving other financial regulators a stronger check on its rules is a legitimate structural critique. The bill's design, however, handed that check to regulators whose statutory duty is the health of the banks being regulated, and excluded the CFPB Director from the vote.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains would have flowed almost entirely to banks and other regulated financial firms, in the form of an easier, mandatory process for killing CFPB rules they disliked. The costs would have fallen on the public in the form of weaker, more reversible consumer protections — the rules governing mortgages, credit cards, and debt collection could have been voided by a simple majority of banking regulators using a test about institutional soundness rather than consumer harm. The accountability argument for checking a powerful agency is real, but this bill's mechanism placed the check in the hands of the industry's own prudential regulators, so the balance clearly favors concentrated financial interests over ordinary consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Duffy (R-WI) introduced the bill on March 4, 2015, with Reps. Randy Neugebauer (R-TX) and Andy Barr (R-KY) as original cosponsors; it picked up one more Republican cosponsor for a total of three.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Financial Services on the day it was introduced; no committee or floor action of any kind followed.

The bill sat in committee until the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the existing law — under which the Council may set aside a CFPB rule only by a two-thirds vote and only when it risks the whole banking system — remained unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyday consumers came out ahead: the CFPB's rulemaking authority and the high bar for overriding its rules stayed intact, and the banks that backed the bill gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers whose CFPB protections remained in place

for.name: Rep. Sean Duffy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to make it easier for bank regulators to override CFPB rules.

for.name: Reps. Randy Neugebauer and Andy Barr
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as original cosponsors alongside Duffy.

for.name: Banking industry trade groups
for.what_they_did: Fought throughout this period to weaken the CFPB's independence and give prudential bank regulators greater power over its rules.

against.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup; the record shows no committee or floor action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party breakdown exists; all four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans.

industries.industry: Large banks and insured depository institutions
industries.note: If passed, banks could have used a member agency petition to force the Council to strike CFPB rules on a simple majority vote, with a standard about individual institutions' sound operations instead of system-wide risk. Their gain comes directly at the expense of consumer rules that constrain their practices.

The bill would have stripped the Bureau's rules of finality: its Director would be excluded from override votes, its rules could be voided on a laxer standard at any time, and the Bureau would have to weigh bank soundness in every rule. The Bureau's role is protecting consumers, so weakening it runs against the public's interest.

industries.industry: Payday lenders and consumer finance companies
industries.note: Nonbank lenders targeted by CFPB rules would also have benefited, since any Council set-aside would relieve them of the rule as well as banks.
